title: Workers in the Constitution of India
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Where the Constitution speaks about freedom of association, fair wages and workers' participation.
body:
The Constitution of India does not contain a long chapter on labour, but it speaks about workers in several important places: in the list of Fundamental Rights, in the Directive Principles of State Policy, and in the division of powers between Parliament and the States. Knowing these provisions helps in reading any debate on labour law, because most arguments about wages, unions or social security eventually go back to them. Republic Day, 26 January, is a fitting occasion to read them again.

## Fundamental Rights that touch workers

Fundamental Rights can be enforced directly in the High Courts and the Supreme Court. Three of them bear on work.

- **Article 19(1)(c)** guarantees all citizens the right to form associations or unions. The final text also includes co-operative societies, which were added during the drafting stage. This is the constitutional base of trade unionism. The right is not unlimited: Article 19(4) permits the State to make reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, public order or morality. The original 1950 text listed only public order and morality; the sovereignty ground was added later.
- **Article 23** prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labour. Article 23(2) allows the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes, but it may not discriminate on grounds of religion, race, caste or class when it does so.
- **Article 24** says that no child below the age of fourteen shall be employed in any factory or mine or in any other hazardous employment. The Constituent Assembly adopted this article on 3 December 1948, the same day it adopted Article 23.

Two points are worth noticing. First, Article 19(1)(c) protects the right to *form* a union; it does not by itself say that an employer must recognise or bargain with it. That is a matter for ordinary law, which is one reason recognition rules in the Industrial Relations Code attract so much attention. Second, Articles 23 and 24 describe what must not happen at work. The positive side, what the State should try to bring about, lies in the Directive Principles.

## Directive Principles that speak to workers

The Directive Principles are not enforceable in court, but the Constitution says they are fundamental in the governance of the country, and that the State should apply them in making laws. Several relate directly to workers.

- **Article 39** sets out principles of policy. Among them are equal pay for equal work for both men and women, and a requirement that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused. It also asks that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter work unsuited to their age or strength, and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation.
- **Article 41** speaks of the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement. It is qualified by the phrase "within the limits of its economic capacity and development", so the obligation is real but conditional on resources.
- **Article 42** requires the State to make provision for just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. The Constituent Assembly passed it in November 1948 without debate or amendment.
- **Article 43** directs the State to endeavour to secure a living wage and conditions of work that ensure a decent standard of life and leisure, for agricultural, industrial and other workers. It also asks the State to promote cottage industries in rural areas. In the Assembly debate of 23 November 1948, members argued that economic democracy was necessary for political democracy, and added agricultural workers and cottage industries to the draft.
- **Article 43A**, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, directs the State to take steps to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations. It was not part of the original Constitution.

## Why "directive" does not mean "optional"

Because the Directive Principles cannot be enforced as such, some people dismiss them as wishes. That is too simple. They guide Parliament and the State legislatures in making laws and they influence how courts read ordinary statutes. A law on minimum wages, for example, is the State's attempt to carry out the direction on a living wage. A maternity benefit law carries out Article 42. When courts examine whether a labour law is reasonable, these articles often supply the yardstick.

The qualifier in Article 41, on economic capacity, also shows how the Constitution balances aspiration and resources. It does not promise an instant right to work; it asks the State to move towards one as far as its means allow.

## Labour on the Concurrent List

Labour is a subject on the Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule, so both Parliament and the State legislatures can make laws on it. The relevant entries are brief but wide. Entry 22 covers trade unions and industrial and labour disputes. Entry 23 covers social security and social insurance, and employment and unemployment. Entry 24 covers the welfare of labour, including conditions of work, provident funds, employers' liability, workmen's compensation, invalidity and old-age pensions, and maternity benefits.

This division explains why the Labour Codes are central laws that States then support with their own rules. Under the Codes, the "appropriate government" for many matters is the Central Government and for others the State Government, and States frame rules for the subjects that fall to them. It also explains why the same worker may find that a central law sets the floor, while a State sets details such as the actual minimum wage rate for a local industry.

## What this means for BMS's demands

When BMS asks for minimum wages, social security or workers' participation, these are not only demands. They connect to directions the Constitution itself gives the State. A few examples show the link.

- A demand for a **living wage** and a statutory floor wage echoes Article 43.
- A demand for **pensions and health cover** for the old and the unorganised echoes Article 41 and Article 39(e).
- A demand for **maternity relief** and humane conditions echoes Article 42.
- A demand for **workers' participation in management**, which BMS places within its motto *Labourise the Industry*, echoes Article 43A.
- The right to organise, which BMS exercises in every one of its unions, rests on Article 19(1)(c).

BMS also argues that scheme workers such as Anganwadi and ASHA workers, who do public work but are called volunteers, should be recognised as workers. The Constitution's language on just and humane conditions of work is a natural starting point for that argument, though courts have decided the question of their legal status on narrower grounds.

## What remains to be done

Reading the Constitution on labour also shows the gaps between text and practice. The right to work in Article 41 is a direction and not an enforceable right. Workers' participation in management, directed in 1976, has not become a general feature of Indian industry. And the right to form unions does not guarantee that every worker, especially in the unorganised and gig economy, can in practice form or join one. These are questions on which readers will meet differing views, and later posts on the Labour Codes will look at how the new laws handle them.
